items.note: Gazetteer preface: Vidisha has a hoary past; referred to in Epics, Puranas and Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical literature; the Heliodoros Pillar at Besnagar and the magnificent temples at Gyaraspur, Udayapur and Badoh symbolise the district's cultural heritage.
Vidisha as a rich trading centre on the cross-roads of two trade routes (Mathura to Pratisthan; Pataliputra to Bharukachchha), with Kalidasa's Meghaduta reference.
Association with Emperor Asoka: he married Devi, a banker's daughter, at Vidisha; sentence continues on the next page.

items.note: Vidisha District's latitude and longitude, position in the eastern part of the fertile Malwa region and elliptical shape.
Earliest reference to Vidisha in the Ramayana; Mahabharata mention; Besnagar identified with ancient Vidisha and its literary forms; tradition of Raja Rukmangada naming the town Vishvanagar.

Brihat Samhita mention; after the destruction of Besnagar on the western side of the Betwa (after the 7th century A.D.) a new town arose on the eastern bank, known as Bhailaswamin, later corrupted to Bhilsa (seen by Al Beruni in the 11th century).

Administrative history: Vidisha (Bhilsa) a tahsil of Isagarh pargana in Gwalior State; raised to a District in 1904 with Vidisha and Basoda tahsils; enlarged in 1949 and 1956; town and District renamed Vidisha.

items.note: Vidisha (Bhilsa) was part of Prant Malwa of the former Gwalior State; now divided into five tahsils including Basoda.
Vidisha lies on the Vindhyachal plateau; most of it is in the valley of the Betwa, flowing south to north, bordered by the Garhi-Teonda and Ganari-Raghoghar ranges.
Rich black soil in the valleys from basalt silt; the tract is one of the major wheat-growing tracts of Malwa.
Eastern range has sedimentary rocks, sandstone and limestone of very high quality; Gyaraspur and Udaipur are located amidst the west-side foothills of this range.
The district lies in the Yamuna drainage basin with the Betwa Basin proper between two sub-water divides.
The Betwa is a river of great antiquity, third largest of the Malwa region; enters the district 6 km south of Vidisha.
Leaves the district after about 112 km; tributaries on left and right banks; Besnagar is a place of great archaeological importance along the river.
The Kethan, last significant left-bank tributary of the Betwa, rises near Sironj and is tapped for a medium-size irrigation tank.
The Nion drains the southern part of the district and joins the Betwa near Sumer; the Keotan joins the Betwa on its right bank within the district.
Geological formations of the district: alluvium, laterite and Deccan Trap; alluvium along the Betwa forms steep cliffs in the north.
Deccan Trap is the most widespread rock formation, basalt with inter-trappean limestone.
The District provides inexhaustible reserves of building materials.
Upper Vindhyan sandstones are excellent, extensively quarried building material; Kaimur sandstone strongest for massive structures; the softer sandstone used for delicate carving.
Highly ferruginous laterite cappings were tapped as a source of iron-ore for indigenous furnaces.
Groundwater supply is problematical in the Deccan trap country; shallow wells yield needed water except in a drought summer; water level 6 to 12 m.
Forests cover about two-fifths of the district, mostly on hill ranges and steep slopes.
Seismically the district is in a zone with only slight intensity earthquakes, with fringe effects of great distant earthquakes.
